can_fail_a.instructions: Break the behaviour this test names, in the code under test only. Does the test then fail? Any break counts, including one that changes only the shape of the result or makes the call throw.

criteria.true: the test fails when the named behaviour is broken
criteria.false: the test still passes when the named behaviour is broken

can_fail_b.instructions: Does this test keep passing however the code under test breaks the behaviour this test names?

criteria.true: no break of the named behaviour makes the test fail
criteria.false: some break of the named behaviour makes the test fail

can_fail_c.instructions: If the behaviour this test names regresses, does the test fail?

criteria.true: a regression in that behaviour makes the test fail
criteria.false: a regression in that behaviour leaves the test passing

asserts_a.instructions: Taken together, what do the assertions of this test check about the code under test? Pick the kind of the strongest assertion.

criteria.behaviour: an output value or effect of the code under test, compared with an expected value the test fixes itself: a literal, a constant the test file declares, or a value the test computes without calling the code under test
criteria.hardcoded-data: an expected value taken from the code under test itself, such as a constant it exports or a second call to the same code, so both sides agree by construction
criteria.input-only: its own input or setup, not what the code under test produced
criteria.shape-only: only the type, length, keys, presence, or definedness of a result, not its content, even when compared with a literal such as a list of key names
criteria.interaction-only: only that a mock or spy was called, how often, or with what, not the result it stands in for
criteria.nothing: no assertion, a tautology such as true === true, or only that the call did not throw

asserts_b.instructions: What does the strongest assertion in this test check?

criteria.nothing: no assertion, a tautology such as true === true, or only that the call did not throw
criteria.interaction-only: only that a mock or spy was called, how often, or with what, not the result it stands in for
criteria.shape-only: only the type, length, keys, presence, or definedness of a result, not its content, even when compared with a literal such as a list of key names
criteria.input-only: its own input or setup, not what the code under test produced
criteria.hardcoded-data: an expected value taken from the code under test itself, such as a constant it exports or a second call to the same code, so both sides agree by construction
criteria.behaviour: an output value or effect of the code under test, compared with an expected value the test fixes itself: a literal, a constant the test file declares, or a value the test computes without calling the code under test

positive_a.instructions: Does at least one assertion name a value that the code under test must produce, such as a literal, an object, a thrown error with its message, or the true or false result the name asks for? An empty array, string, or object, null, or undefined does not count, even written as a literal.

criteria.true: at least one assertion names a value that must be produced
criteria.false: every assertion checks only that something is null, undefined, empty, or did not throw

positive_b.instructions: Does every assertion in this test check only that something is null, undefined, empty, or did not throw? An expected empty array, string, or object counts as empty.

criteria.true: every assertion checks only that something is null, undefined, empty, or did not throw
criteria.false: at least one assertion names a value that must be produced

runs_a.instructions: Does this test run, and does every other test in the file run? Read the test head, the scope field, and the flags field. A skip, todo, or skipIf marker, or an x prefix such as xit or xdescribe, on the test or on a describe around it stops this test. An only or focus marker anywhere in the file, such as it.only, fit, or fdescribe, shows as the flag focus-in-file and leaves other tests out.

criteria.true: this test runs, and no marker in the file leaves another test out
criteria.false: a marker stops this test, or a marker in the file leaves other tests out

runs_b.instructions: Does a marker stop this test or narrow the run? Read the test head, the scope field, and the flags field. A skip, todo, or skipIf marker, or an x prefix such as xit or xdescribe, on the test or on a describe around it stops this test. An only or focus marker anywhere in the file, such as it.only, fit, or fdescribe, shows as the flag focus-in-file and leaves other tests out.

criteria.true: a marker stops this test, or a marker in the file leaves other tests out
criteria.false: this test runs, and no marker in the file leaves another test out

type.instructions: What type of test is this? If the name cites a bug or an issue, answer regression. If the test pins current output as a baseline before a change, answer characterization. If it only checks that something runs or exists, answer smoke. Otherwise answer by scope: unit, integration, or e2e.

criteria.unit: one small unit in isolation, with its collaborators mocked or absent
criteria.integration: several units together, such as code with a real database, filesystem, or module
criteria.regression: the name cites a past bug or issue that the test keeps from returning
criteria.e2e: drives the whole system through its public interface
criteria.smoke: only checks that something runs or exists, at a coarse level
criteria.characterization: pins current output as a baseline before a change

observable.instructions: Does the assertion read an output or an effect that a caller of the public interface could see? A return value, a thrown error, a change the caller can read back, or a message sent through an injected port is observable. A private field, an underscore member, an internal helper call, or the order of internal calls is not.

criteria.true: it asserts an output or effect a caller could see
criteria.false: it asserts a private internal, an internal helper call, or internal call order

conditional.instructions: Does every assertion in this test always run? Answer no when a branch, a loop over a value that may be empty, an early return, or a try/catch can leave an assertion unrun or swallow its failure.

criteria.true: every assertion always runs
criteria.false: a branch, loop, early return, or catch can leave an assertion unrun or swallow its failure

isolated.instructions: Does this test read only values that it builds itself, or that a hook in fixtures builds before each test? Answer no when it reads a value that another test must set, or mutable state in setup that is shared with other tests and that no hook resets. An object the file declares once, such as a registry, that this test reads but another test fills, is shared state.

criteria.true: it builds what it reads, so it passes alone and in any order
criteria.false: it reads state that another test sets, or mutable state shared with other tests

controlled.instructions: Does the test create or fake every external thing it reads, such as a file, a server, an environment variable, or the clock? Answer yes when it reads none.

criteria.true: it creates or fakes every external resource it reads, or it reads none
criteria.false: it reads a file, server, environment variable, or clock that it does not create or fake

specific.instructions: Does the assertion pin the expected value with an exact matcher, such as toBe, toEqual, toStrictEqual, or toThrow with a message? Answer no when it uses a weak form that also passes on wrong output: toBeDefined, toBeTruthy, typeof, Array.isArray, a length, a bound such as toBeGreaterThan(0), or a boolean folded from a comparison.

criteria.true: the assertion pins the expected value
criteria.false: the assertion is a weak form that also passes on wrong output

named.instructions: Does the test's name state the behaviour it checks, rather than a vague label such as works, test1, should be fine, or only the name of the unit, such as add or parser?

criteria.true: the name says which behaviour the test checks
criteria.false: the name is a vague label that does not say which behaviour the test checks

deterministic.instructions: Does this test give the same result on every run? It does not when it reads the real clock or real randomness, calls the network, waits on a sleep, or relies on an order nothing guarantees. A clock, timer, or random source that the test fakes or seeds is under its control and is fine.

criteria.true: the result is the same on every run of the same code
criteria.false: the result can differ between runs of the same code

one_thing.instructions: Does this test check one behaviour, rather than several unrelated behaviours at once? Several assertions on one result count as one behaviour. Several actions on different units, each with its own assertion, count as several.

criteria.true: it checks one behaviour
criteria.false: it is an eager test that checks several unrelated behaviours

name_matches.instructions: Does the test body assert the behaviour its name states? If the name states no behaviour, answer no. A body that checks only that the result is truthy, defined, or of a type does not assert the behaviour.

criteria.true: the body asserts the behaviour the name promises
criteria.false: the name states no behaviour, or it states one and the body asserts something else or something trivial

resilient.instructions: Would a refactor that keeps the public behaviour of the code under test keep this test green? Answer no when the test imports an internal module, spies on an internal helper, reads a private field, pins the order of internal calls, or pins an internal structure in a snapshot.

criteria.true: the test reaches the code only through its public interface and asserts only results, so a refactor keeps it green
criteria.false: the test pins an internal module, helper, field, call order, or structure, so a refactor breaks it

diagnostic.instructions: Does each assertion compare a value with a matcher that reports the expected and the received value, such as toBe or toEqual? A bare boolean check such as expect(a === b).toBe(true) or assert(ok), a comparison folded into one boolean, or one assertion repeated in a loop with no index hides which value was wrong.

criteria.true: each failure shows the received value and the expected value
criteria.false: a failure shows only true or false, or cannot say which value failed

fixture.instructions: Does the test, or a hook in fixtures or code in setup, build the data the test reads, and no more? Answer no when the test reads a value that nothing shown builds, or when the fixture holds far more than the behaviour needs.

criteria.true: it builds the data it reads, and only that
criteria.false: it reads a value that nothing shown builds, or it leans on a fixture far larger than it needs

fast.instructions: Does the test finish without a sleep, a poll, a network or disk call, or a loop over a large input? An await on an in-memory promise is fine.

criteria.true: it does none of these
criteria.false: it sleeps, polls, calls the network or disk, or computes over a large input

readable.instructions: Does the test show the input, the action, and the expected result? Answer no when the input or the expected value comes from a helper, an import, or a name that nothing shown defines, or when the comparison hides in a boolean.

criteria.true: the input, the action, and the expected result are visible in the test
criteria.false: the input or the expected value is hidden, or the comparison hides in a boolean

magic_number.instructions: Can a reader tell what each literal in the assertion means from the test name, the input, or a name beside it? A plain result of the input, such as 180 seconds for 3 minutes, is fine. A code, a flag, or a total that the reader must look up in the code under test is a magic number.

criteria.true: the meaning of each literal is clear from the test
criteria.false: a literal must be looked up in the code under test

reads_output.instructions: Does the assertion read the value the code under test produced, rather than its own input, its setup, or only that no error was thrown? A test that asserts its argument is unchanged counts as yes only when its name says the code must not change it.

criteria.true: it asserts the returned or observed output
criteria.false: it asserts its own input, its setup, or merely that the call did not throw

automated.instructions: Does this test reach a pass or fail with no person doing or reading anything?

criteria.true: it is self-checking and unattended
criteria.false: it has no assertion and only prints, or it waits for a person to act or to read its output

restores.instructions: Does the test leave every global, environment variable, timer, module mock, spy, and shared object that the file or its setup declares as it found them? A restore in an after hook in fixtures counts. A test that changes none of these counts as yes.

criteria.true: it changes none of these, or it restores what it changes
criteria.false: it leaves a global, environment variable, timer, mock, spy, or shared object changed

verdict.instructions: Overall, is this test a real guard? Slop: it asserts nothing, or it cannot fail at all, such as a tautology or two sides that both come from the code under test. Weak: it asserts only a shape, a mock call, an absence, or its own input passed straight through, so it misses most ways the named behaviour can break. Good: it asserts a value or effect that the named behaviour decides. Strong: good, with an exact expected value that would fail loudly. An expected value the test computes itself without the code under test, such as a sorted copy of its input, is a real expected value. Judge only what the assertions check: a smell from the other definitions, such as slow, flaky, the real clock, randomness, the network, a manual step, uncontrolled, a vague name, a magic number, or a state leak, does not lower the level.
